newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African-EU trade negotiations seen starting soon.
newsitem.headline: S.African-EU trade negotiations seen starting soon.

text.p: Preliminary discussions on the South African mandate for free trade area negotiations with the European Union (EU) were expected to start towards the end of November, Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin said.
Wrapping up a snap debate in parliament on the negotiations, Erwin said they were expected to be "tough" and South Africans should not expect miracles.
He said government, business and unions had prepared the mandate with great thoroughness.
"(I am) confident that when we go back to the EU, there will be no possibility of being faulted on a lack of homework," Erwin said.
Several legislators expressed concern that the negotiations could result in an agreement that benefitted the EU more than South Africa while damaging the economies of other Southern African states.

They cited the fact that while EU agricultural products were heavily subsidised, South Africa was being expected to provide virtually free access to those products which could wipe out local beef and dairy products industries.
Erwin said that it had to be recognised that the EU was South Africa's largest trading partner but that South Africa was determined to ensure that the region as a whole benefitted.
He said that once the EU decided not to offer South Africa access to the Lome Convention for developing countries, it was inevitable that negotiations would be complicated.

Instead of being on the same footing as its neighbours in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and South African Customs Union (SACU), South Africa had to weigh up how a free trade agreement would affect them.
As neighbouring states were rapidly building up trade deficits with South Africa, the country had to open its markets to a higher degree and encourage investment in SADC.
As a result, trade agreements with these states were being renegotiated, and would probably need special protocols on products such as sugar, steel, automobiles and a range of agricultural products.
These had to be complementary to any trade deal with the EU.
On the length of time it had taken to finalise South Africa's mandate, Erwin said it would have been "extremely unwise to move faster...we had to do our homework."
